description: Verified ground truth for backtesting Signal's forecaster against real devtool launches. Each case pairs a public pre-announcement artifact with the announcement that followed it. Every date and URL below was checked against the vendor's own blog — nothing here is inferred, and a case that could not be verified from a primary source was left out rather than estimated.
verification_method: For each case: (1) locate the official announcement post and read its publication date from the vendor's own site; (2) locate the earliest public artifact that signalled the same work and read its date the same way; (3) record both URLs. Cases where step 2 could not be satisfied from a primary source are excluded.
known_gaps: Two positive cases is far too few to produce a meaningful accuracy number. This file is a starting point, not a benchmark.

No control cases yet. A control is a window of routine activity where no launch followed, and asserting 'nothing happened' needs the same primary-source rigour as asserting something did. Fabricating controls would be worse than having none, because they would silently inflate any specificity figure computed from this file.

Both cases use blog posts as the pre-announcement artifact. The GitHub collector's real thesis is that branches, pull request titles and new repositories lead even those — cases resting on that evidence need repository archaeology that has not been done here.

pre_announcement.what_it_was: Deno published a 2.0 release candidate describing it as the largest update since 1.0, naming the Node process global, deno add/deno remove, WebGPU and FFI stabilisation, and CommonJS support.
pre_announcement.why_it_is_a_signal: A release candidate enumerating breaking changes is a commitment to ship, not an exploration. The specific features named here are the ones the launch post led with.

outcome.what_happened: Deno 2 was announced, with long-term support and Node/npm compatibility as the headline.

pre_announcement.what_it_was: Tailwind open-sourced its v4.0 progress and tagged the first public v4.0.0-alpha, describing the new engine previously codenamed Oxide.
pre_announcement.why_it_is_a_signal: A tagged public alpha with a named engine rewrite is the clearest possible statement of what the next major version will be, and it preceded the stable release by most of a year.

outcome.what_happened: Tailwind CSS v4.0 shipped stable, led by build-performance gains and a reimagined configuration model.
